newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. welfare task force seen only drafting options.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. welfare task force seen only drafting options.

text.p: New York's welfare task force, which had planned to give the governor its recommendations, instead is likely to only produce a list of options that will be used to draft a broad plan, a state source said on Thursday.
As a result, the Pataki Administration would seem to have fairly broad discretion about what type of plan it submits, although the outlines can be changed later on.

The Governor has been under pressure to quickly submit at least a basic outline of its welfare program to Washington to ensure it gets as much of its $2.4 billion block grant as it can. The New York City Council has said the state risked losing up to $1 million a day for every day it waited after October 1.

A spokeswoman for Gov. George Pataki, who denied that the state was advancing the process, on Wednesday said New York planned to submit its welfare plan early next week. She was not immediately available to comment on Thursday.
The Republican governor has said he planned to call a special legislative session in December to enact the law needed to put a new welfare program in place.

New York, which had been stressing the thoroughness of the review being conducted by its welfare task force, evidently was surprised at the rudimentary and vague outlines of the plans submitted by other states, the state source explained. The source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, added no further meetings have been scheduled for the task force.

After the bipartisan group began meeting, it became apparent that the Democrat-led Assembly might be reluctant to reveal its hand. The Assembly's reluctance reflected its concern that the various policies were so intertwined that it could not sign off on one without knowing the whole program.

"They said that they were afraid that if they said anything it would look like there was a consensus on things when there wasn't...So after that it moved on to a more general discussion of the outline," the source said.

While the Republican governor's attempt to impose workfare requirements and set time limits stalled this year in the Assembly, another state source appeared confident that the legislature and governor would be able to agree a plan.

"The speaker's position is that the Feds have spoken. They've sort of set the parameters," said the source, who declined to be named. He was referring to Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan. A staffer for Silver declined comment.

To deal with the complex issues posed by the sweeping federal welfare reforms, the state task force set up by Pataki is preparing around 150 pages of charts that set out the new federal law, the old law, and what choices the state can make.

The matrix of options delves into a wide range of options, including whether or not to simply adopt the new five-year time limits set by the federal government, or to add more strict restrictions. For example, some categories of people might be eligible for two years of benefits and others for the full five years, the source explained.

Decentralizing the state welfare program by giving local counties more control but also leaving them liable for any penalites if they fail to meet the new federal standards is another example of the kinds of options that will be included.
